summary:
Ogun State, a state in southern Nigeria, has no protective statute of its own for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, and the sources reviewed record no incident series or enforcement divergence specific to Ogun. The national framework applies in full, and it reaches well beyond marriage.

The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 is the operative national statute. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Criminal exposure attaches at the point of entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

UK travel advice now addresses LGBT+ visitors directly. The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 advisory for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of a 14-year jail term under the 2014 Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, and of possible death-penalty risk under Sharia criminal law in some northern states. That advisory is the national frame for Ogun, a southern state outside the Sharia zone.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing. In August 2024 the beaten body of the 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found along a highway in Abuja (BBC News, 9 August 2024); she had posted about being transgender and working as a sex worker and had expressed fears for her life the previous year. Police said preliminary investigations revealed that the individual was a man fully dressed in female clothing. The killing took place in the federal capital, outside Ogun, and stands as national evidence of lethal violence against transgender people rather than as an Ogun incident.
tangentialFactors:
The only trans-specific imprisonment case in the sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

The risk profile differs sharply by region within Nigeria. The twelve northern states apply Sharia criminal law, under which male sodomy carries the death penalty, while Ogun sits in the south where secular provisions govern and the maximum exposure for same-sex conduct under the SSMPA is 14 years. A visitor transiting northward crosses into a materially harsher penalty regime.

Lethal violence against transgender people has produced official response without prosecution. Six months after the August 2024 killing of Abuja Area Mama, no suspects had been charged (the Dial, February 2025), while the Abuja police chief had ordered a thorough and discreet investigation.

Legislative turbulence around gender expression persists without a settled outcome. Reuters (September 2022) records public fear among transgender Nigerians of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing, and the sources available do not establish whether such proposals have been enacted.
localsOnly:
Ogun residents have no state-level anti-discrimination protection, no hate-crime provision covering gender identity, and no statutory recourse when police invoke the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014. The Act's 10 to 14 year penalties apply to cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, so ordinary shared housing and organising carry criminal exposure.

Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents police invoking the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest, a pattern that residents rather than visitors absorb as routine enforcement. Extortion compounds the exposure: in a documented Lagos case a young man was released only after paying a substantial share of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay.

Transgender residents face the additional uncertainty of where they will be held if detained. Press coverage of the Bobrisky sentence treated the choice between male and female sections as an open administrative question, and an October 2024 panel found that her maximum-security placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, addressing the conditions of her confinement rather than establishing a rule of placement for transgender detainees generally.

Residents who are LGBTQ+ are also targeted by kito gangs through dating apps, where the currency is filmed evidence and threats of outing to family and employers. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than replacing it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted is unresolved. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians feared such proposals, and no source in this inventory confirms their legislative status.

No Ogun-specific incident, arrest or prosecution is documented in these sources. The killing of Abuja Area Mama occurred in the federal capital and the extortion case in Lagos; neither is attributed to Ogun, and no Ogun enforcement record or state-level directive was located.

Whether the Ogun State government has issued any policy, directive or policing instruction on gender identity is not sourced here. The dossier's statement that Ogun has no protective statute rests on the absence of such a statute in the reviewed material rather than on an official confirmation of absence.

Ogun-specific data on access to gender-affirming care, documentation marker changes, and prison placement for transgender detainees is not sourced. The placement question is evidenced only through the Bobrisky case in Lagos.

Figures on the frequency of violence against LGBT+ people in Ogun, and on whether police in Ogun use the SSMPA differently from the patterns documented in Lagos and Abuja, are not available in this inventory.
